messages.content: You check claims about a scientific paper against the evidence each one cites. A claim is supported only if the cited evidence says it AS WRITTEN: the same subject, row, column, setting and number. A correct value attached to the wrong subject or row is NOT supported, and neither is a claim that goes beyond its evidence. Judge only from the cited evidence; figure images are attached where a claim cites a figure. Give a verdict for every claim.

Claims:
1. "The performance of the networks trained by RCE is as good as and sometimes even better than those trained by the traditional CE procedure." -- cites: E1 (Section 4.2): quote "We can see that the performance of the networks trained by RCE is as good as and sometimes even better than those trained by the traditional CE procedure."
2. "ResNet-56 (RCE) has an AUC-score of 89.1, which is higher than ResNet-56 (CE) with an AUC-score of 84.9." -- cites: E3 (Section Table 4): quote "Res.-56 (RCE) 89.1 84.9"
3. "The evidence does not directly compare ResNet-32 (CE) and ResNet-32 (RCE) on the MNIST dataset." -- cites: E1 (Section 4.2): quote "We ﬁrst evaluate in the normal setting, where we implement Resnet-32 and Resnet-56 [ 15 ] on both datasets. For each network, we use both the CE and RCE as the training objectives, trained by the same settings as He et al. [16] ."

Cited evidence:
[E1] (text, Section 4.2, page 6): We ﬁrst evaluate in the normal setting, where we implement Resnet-32 and Resnet-56 [ 15 ] on both datasets. For each network, we use both the CE and RCE as the training objectives, trained by the same settings as He et al. [16] . The number of training steps for both objectives is set to be 20,000 on MNIST and 90,000 on CIFAR-10. Hereafter for notation simplicity, we will indicate the training procedure used after the model name of a trained network, e.g., Resnet-32 (CE). Similarly, we indicate the training procedure and omit the name of the target network after an attacking method, e.g., FGSM (CE). Table 1 shows the test error rates, where the thresholding test strategy is disabled and all the points receive their predicted labels. We can see that the performance of the networks trained by RCE is as good as and sometimes even better than those trained by the traditional CE procedure. Note that we apply the same training hyperparameters (e.g., learning rates and decay factors) for both the CE and RCE procedures, which suggests that RCE is easy to optimize and does not require much extra effort on tuning hyperparameters.
[E3] (text, Section Table 4, page 8): Table 4: AUC-scores ( 10 − 2 ) on CIFAR-10. Resnet-32 is the substitute model and Resnet-56 is the target model. Res.-32 (CE) Res.-32 (RCE) Res.-56 (CE) 75.0 90.8 Res.-56 (RCE) 89.1 84.9

verdicts.reason: The evidence in E1 directly states that the performance of the networks trained by RCE is as good as and sometimes even better than those trained by the traditional CE procedure.
The evidence in E3 provides the AUC-scores for ResNet-56 (RCE) as 89.1 and ResNet-56 (CE) as 84.9, which directly supports the claim that ResNet-56 (RCE) has a higher AUC-score than ResNet-56 (CE).

The evidence in E1 does not directly compare ResNet-32 (CE) and ResNet-32 (RCE) on the MNIST dataset. It only mentions the evaluation of ResNet-32 and ResNet-56 on both datasets with both CE and RCE as training objectives. The comparison of ResNet-32 (CE) and ResNet-32 (RCE) is not explicitly stated in the evidence.
